news.article_content:
NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia's accounting practices, said two people briefed on the matter, adding to the legal woes facing the scandal-hit chip giant.

The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday reported that the SEC was probing Nvidia but said it could not ascertain the focus of the investigation. The people, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential issues, said SEC enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues at the company.

A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Reuters could not immediately determine when the SEC opened its inquiry or exactly what potential accounting issues the watchdog is examining. Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without resulting in enforcement action.

Still, the accounting focus of the probe, which Reuters is reporting for the first time, increases pressure on Nvidia, whose investors are still reeling from revelations about ousted CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital relationships, including with Alice Huang, who US authorities suspect is a Chinese spy. China has denied she is a spy.

US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible violations of export controls related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the US Justice and Commerce departments said this week.

The crisis has sent shares in Nvidia, a linchpin of the AI boom, tumbling more than a third and stoked calls in Washington for tougher action on tech threats posed by Beijing.

Megaspeed has said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it conducted "lawful business." Reuters has not been able to reach Alice Huang. paragraphs: NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia's accounting practices, said two people briefed on the matter, adding to the legal woes facing the scandal-hit chip giant.

The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday reported that the SEC was probing Nvidia but said it could not ascertain the focus of the investigation. The people, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential issues, said SEC enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues at the company.
A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Reuters could not immediately determine when the SEC opened its inquiry or exactly what potential accounting issues the watchdog is examining. Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without resulting in enforcement action.

Still, the accounting focus of the probe, which Reuters is reporting for the first time, increases pressure on Nvidia, whose investors are still reeling from revelations about ousted CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital relationships, including with Alice Huang, who US authorities suspect is a Chinese spy. China has denied she is a spy.

Alice Huang led Singapore-based Megaspeed, historically a large Nvidia chip customer, people familiar with the matter have said. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible violations of export controls related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the US Justice and Commerce departments said this week.
The crisis has sent shares in Nvidia, a linchpin of the AI boom, tumbling more than a third and stoked calls in Washington for tougher action on tech threats posed by Beijing.

Megaspeed has said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it conducted "lawful business." Reuters has not been able to reach Alice Huang. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a November 8 statement following the reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, without referring to her by name.

The SEC probe is the latest of Nvidia's legal woes. The Justice Department has also been reviewing Nvidia's $12.9-billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face alongside a broader antitrust investigation into the company's acquisitions and practices, Reuters reported last month.
SINGAPORE ACCOUNTING CHANGE BACK IN FOCUS

Last year, Nvidia changed how it reports geographic revenue, using customer headquarters rather than billing addresses, which it said would better reflect the geographic profile of its revenue. The change resulted in Singapore being removed from its geographical breakdown.
The Financial Times, citing company accounts, reported on Tuesday that Nvidia had made the change even as Singapore sales soared to almost half its global revenue.
That accounting shift has drawn renewed press scrutiny in the wake of the Alice Huang scandal.
Southeast Asia has become a hub for chip smuggling to China since the Biden administration barred advanced AI chip exports to that country over concerns they could boost Beijing’s military.

Analysts and investors have also grown increasingly concerned about circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers including Nvidia have pursued complex financial arrangements to help customers fund purchases of their chips and the construction of costly AI infrastructure, such as data centers. Nvidia has backed AI companies and cloud providers and provided guarantees connected to data-center projects that use its equipment.

Critics say such arrangements can make it harder for investors to assess the quality of chipmakers' revenue and their true financial exposure. Speaking to Reuters last month, SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures to ensure issuers are giving investors the full picture on potential risks.

On its Tuesday earnings call, Nvidia's interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress said the company was proud of its role in supporting the AI industry, but would be far more selective moving forward about AI industry financing deals.

The SEC under President Donald Trump has pulled back on enforcement, saying it will focus on bread-and-butter securities fraud, including accounting violations that have long been a mainstay of its enforcement work. It recently launched a new financial reporting and accounting unit within its enforcement division, aimed at developing cases in accounting and auditing areas.

news.title: Nvidia stock plunges 12%, rides longest weekly losing streak since 2008 financial crisis
news.title_en: Nvidia stock plunges 12%, rides longest weekly losing streak since 2008 financial crisis
news.author: Kif Leswing
news.article_content:
The last time Wall Street was this down on Nvidia the chipmaker's flagship product was the GeForce graphics processor for high-end PC video games, and markets were reeling from the global financial crisis.

Nvidia shares fell 12% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day as investors grew increasingly concerned about life after co-founder Jensen Huang. The stock is poised to close lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008.

Shares of Nvidia are down 44% over the period, pushing the company's market cap down by $2.5 trillion. The stock is now trading at around 9.3 times forward earnings, while Advanced Micro Devices is valued at 29 times profit for the next 12 months.

On Friday, Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring potential accounting issues at Nvidia, pushing the stock down further.

Once the most valuable company, now, at a market cap of $3.1 trillion, Nvidia is fourth behind Apple and Microsoft and Alphabet.

Nvidia is reeling from the removal of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12, after multiple reported affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said earlier this week that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms."

But the chipmaker's losing streak started before Nvidia was thrown into crisis as investors worried over the sustainability of the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, and emerging competition in AI chips from Google and AMD.

Even a better-than-expected earnings report, which included an increase to fiscal 2028 guidance, didn't stem the selling. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO, projected revenue growth next fiscal year of 75%, and said that customers aren't going anywhere.

On Tuesday's earnings call with analysts, Kress signed off by saying, "we've got this."In a company meeting the next day, executives told staff that it was moving its yearly review process, which can come with more stock, from March to December.

For investors, one major question is whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and sustain its commanding lead in the AI chip market without its visionary leader. Almost the entire company now is built around the AI trade, a phenomenon that began taking hold just four years ago with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT.

Before that, Nvidia's primary business was selling graphics cards used for video games. In mid-2008, the last time the stock was this deep into a weekly losing streak, Nvidia was generating less than $1 billion per quarter. Now it pulls in more than $1 billion per day. Despite interim CEO Colette Kress's optimistic projections, market sentiment remains anxious regarding leadership stability and competitive pressures.

The discussions remain ongoing and could still conclude without an agreement, Bloomberg reported. Should a deal materialize, it would represent the inaugural major deployment for Helix, which launched in June under former Amazon Web Services chief executive Adam Selipsky after raising roughly $11 billion from KKR's balance sheet alongside backers including Nvidia Corp. and the Kuwait Investment Authority.

EdgeCore brings a substantial footprint to the table, boasting more than 2.27 gigawatts of capacity leased and under development across key U.S. markets in Virginia, Arizona, Nevada, and California. For KKR, acquiring EdgeCore would bolster a sprawling data center portfolio that already includes CyrusOne and reinforce its commitment to AI infrastructure following its participation in a $500 billion chip-financing pact with Nvidia and Wall Street peers earlier this year. Meanwhile, a sale would offer a lucrative exit for Partners Group, which acquired EdgeCore in 2022 with an initial $1.2 billion capital commitment before injecting an additional $1.9 billion to scale its operations.

The talks unfold against a shifting backdrop for data center operators and their financial sponsors. Industry sentiment has recently been tested by heightened regulatory scrutiny following Democratic gains in the midterm elections, increased caution from banks managing a glut of AI-related debt, and leadership upheaval at strategic partner Nvidia following this month's ouster of CEO Jensen Huang.

Ultimately, a completed transaction would establish a closely watched valuation benchmark for buyout firms seeking liquidity from early AI infrastructure bets. Many institutional investors have struggled to price data center assets still awaiting power grid connections and regulatory permits, leaving private equity sponsors searching for viable exit pathways as the sector matures.

news.title: Take-Two says GTA VI generated $3.79B in day-one sales, surpassing the $2.9B lifetime box-office gross of the highest-grossing film Avengers: Endgame (Jennifer Maas/Variety)
news.title_en: Take-Two says GTA VI generated $3.79B in day-one sales, surpassing the $2.9B lifetime box-office gross of the highest-grossing film Avengers: Endgame (Jennifer Maas/Variety)

inline_images.caption: Rockstar Games
inline_images.alt: Rockstar Games

news.author: Variety
news.article_content:
Crime pays: Rockstar Games’ “Grand Theft Auto 6″ preorder and first-day sales reached $3.79 billion, the game developer announced Friday.

Per Rockstar Games parent company Take-Two Interactive, that total sets “a new record for entertainment across any medium” and makes “GTA 6” “the biggest entertainment launch in history.”

For the sake of comparison, Sony Pictures’ “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” reaped $2.52 billion at the global box office in 2026, the No. 1 movie of the year to date. Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster “The Odyssey” has taken in just over $1.8 billion to date.

On its first day of release, “GTA 6” made roughly as much as James Cameron’s last two “Avatar” movies, “The Way of Water” and “Fire and Ash,” have grossed combined. With just Day 1 sales, “GTA 6” has already out-grossed the highest grossing movie of all time, “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion), in one day.

“GTA 6” launched Thursday for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S and was also available on Xbox One via Xbox’s Cloud Gaming service. The game retails at $80 for the standard edition and $100 for the ultimate version. Preorders for “GTA 6” opened June 25.

With a reported total gameplay time of approximately 80 hours to complete its main storyline, “GTA 6” follows duo Jason and Lucia as they navigate their way through criminal life in the fictional Leonida.

“GTA 6” has reached a 99 Metacritic score (tying it for the highest-rated video game of all time) and received a nomination for Game of the Year at The Game Awards this December.

“It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI,’” Rockstar Games president and founder Sam Houser said. “We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.”

news.title: Jensen Huang’s ‘Lying’ Alarmed Nvidia Board Ahead of His Resignation
news.title_en: Jensen Huang’s ‘Lying’ Alarmed Nvidia Board Ahead of His Resignation
news.author: Lauren Goode and Paresh Dave
news.article_content:
Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple issues” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors, according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members.

While Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board announced an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy.

But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf.

According to sources, members of the board had asked Huang about Alice Huang after The New York Times first reported in October 2025 that Nvidia had an unusually robust business relationship with a Singapore-based data center company named Megaspeed, where Alice Huang worked. Jensen Huang at the time denied any inappropriate relationship with Alice Huang to the board, sources tell WIRED.

After the affair came to light, the board was incensed, these people say. A source familiar with the board’s thinking told WIRED that while these board members view issues of national security as “important” and “ongoing,” the primary driver behind Huang’s ouster was “the lying.”

“It was a matter of integrity and trust,” this person said.

In recent days, board members, including chair Harvey Jones, have tried to quell the discourse about Huang’s possible return to Nvidia by emphasizing that Huang's behavior flew in the face of Nvidia’s policies and corporate governance rules, sources tell WIRED. While previous reporting by WIRED and other news outlets have outlined factors that Jones has said played into the board’s decision, the primary motivation hadn’t been previously specified.

paragraphs: Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple issues” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors, according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members.

While Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board announced an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy.

But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf.

According to sources, members of the board had asked Huang about Alice Huang after The New York Times first reported in October 2025 that Nvidia had an unusually robust business relationship with a Singapore-based data center company named Megaspeed, where Alice Huang worked. Jensen Huang at the time denied any inappropriate relationship with Alice Huang to the board, sources tell WIRED.

After the affair came to light, the board was incensed, these people say. A source familiar with the board’s thinking told WIRED that while these board members view issues of national security as “important” and “ongoing,” the primary driver behind Huang’s ouster was “the lying.”
“It was a matter of integrity and trust,” this person said.

In recent days, board members, including chair Harvey Jones, have tried to quell the discourse about Huang’s possible return to Nvidia by emphasizing that Huang's behavior flew in the face of Nvidia’s policies and corporate governance rules, sources tell WIRED. While previous reporting by WIRED and other news outlets have outlined factors that Jones has said played into the board’s decision, the primary motivation hadn’t been previously specified.

Board chair Harvey Jones did not respond to a WIRED request for comment. A spokesperson for Nvidia, John Rizzo, declined to comment. John Fisher, vice president at the communications firm Trident, which is representing Huang, declined to comment except to say that Huang voluntarily resigned from his positions at Nvidia.

For Nvidia’s board, the possibility that Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government poses a bigger problem than an executive’s personal misconduct. If she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, the scandal isn’t just about Huang’s alleged “lack of candor,” but a potential security and governance crisis.

Already the scandal has given China hawks grist to call for tighter controls on US business dealings with China. In addition, multiple government agencies and offices have called for investigations into what the former Nvidia CEO may have known about the company’s chips getting into China. The company’s general counsel Tim Teter has also been called to Washington, DC to testify, as government officials try to find out more about Nvidia’s possible flouting of export controls.

Nvidia and Huang are also facing several shareholder lawsuits, alleging the CEO and the company made misleading statements about dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed. Other Silicon Valley investors have publicly raised concerns about insufficient corporate governance and executive oversight by the board.

In the company’s all-hands meeting on November 18, board chair Jones said it was “not an easy decision to accept [Huang’s] resignation,” according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “However, the disclosure of personal behavior and a lack of candor inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and values made this a necessary decision.”

Meanwhile, fans and supporters of Huang, including thousands of Nvidia employees and Elon Musk, have continued to call for his return to Nvidia. Huang himself has said he would be “honored” to come back as CEO. On Friday, US President Donald Trump renewed his call for Huang to have another chance. “He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump told reporters. “I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology.”

The news outlet Semafor reported that a small faction of Nvidia’s board of directors has pushed to bring Huang back as well. Jones has not responded to WIRED’s inquiries about the board’s reported division on the topic of Huang’s return.

Some employees are miffed at how quickly the board accepted Huang’s resignation, insisting the longtime leader must have been the victim of a coordinated campaign intended to unseat him. “We feel like they forced his hands to resign,” says one person on the business side at Nvidia. “We don’t understand why the board is so adamant about not giving him a second chance.”

At the all-hands meeting, interim CEO Colette Kress said employees’ biggest concern was Nvidia’s falling share price. The next biggest concern was the board’s decision to oust Huang. But while she addressed the first by moving up pay raises, she offered no promise on sharing results of the board’s investigation into Huang or its deliberations about him.
“The ship has sinked but there’s no plan to be transparent about what happened,” says one computer scientist working at Nvidia. “It feels like a black box.”

news.title: Signal blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and Android to stop AI agents from reading private chats
news.title_en: Signal blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and Android to stop AI agents from reading private chats
news.author: Manuel Uth
news.article_content:
Signal is restricting screenshots to stop AI agents from reading private chats. The app blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and triggers protection on supported Android versions when an AI assistant tries to access the screen. Signal warned Reuters of an "existential threat"to privacy.

OS-level AI like Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence can capture screen content to complete user tasks. That undermines end-to-end encryption by letting agents pull decrypted messages straight from the display and process them externally.

Meta's AI agent Muse recently captured Signal content on Android and macOS through broad setup permissions, including accessibility tools and screenshots on macOS. Meta says this happened only with explicit user permission.

Signal already blocked Microsoft's Recall on Windows but calls its defenses incomplete: macOS screenshots can't be reliably blocked, and AI access to file systems and notifications remains a risk. Signal says Apple, Google, and Microsoft should make it easy to block AI agents from apps entirely.

news.title: Canada Retail Sales Tracking Largest Decline Since Feb. 2025
news.title_en: Canada Retail Sales Tracking Largest Decline Since Feb. 2025

inline_images.caption: Canadian Mortgage Trends: Canada
inline_images.alt: Canadian Mortgage Trends: Canada

news.author: Bloomberg
news.article_content:
Canadian retail spending is expected to have declined in October, following a 0.8% increase in September led by gasoline stations and fuel vendors.

A preliminary estimate points to a 1.5% decrease in retail sales last month, which would be the largest decline since February 2025.

Sales in September increased in five out of nine subsectors, and rose by 6.9% at gasoline stations and fuel vendors. That increase was largely driven by higher prices, as sales in volume terms increased by a more modest 1.6%.

Economists surveyed by Bloomberg had expected retail sales increased by 0.7% in September.

Core retail sales, which exclude gasoline stations and fuel vendors as well as motor vehicle and parts dealers, increased by 0.1%. In volume terms, sales were also up by 0.1%.

The largest decline in core retail sales was food and beverage retailers, which was led by a 0.5% decline at grocery stores, following a 1% increase in August.

Building material and garden equipment and supplies dealers declined by 1.3%, while furniture, home furnishings electronics and appliances retailers decreased by the same magnitude.

Meanwhile, retail sales increased by 1.2% in the third quarter. In volume terms, they rose by 1% over the three-month period.

The expected decline in October retail sales provides further evidence of weakening to start the fourth quarter, said CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham.

“While the 1.5% decline estimated for October will partly reflect lower gasoline prices, most of that move lower in pump prices has actually occurred in November rather than October, and as a result this advance estimate suggests a decline in volumes as well,” Grantham said in a note to investors.

The Canadian economy — including consumer spending — has remained largely resilient throughout the U.S. trade war. However, growth is expected to slow in the second half of the year after the dispute escalated and more tariffs were imposed by both countries.

The labour market has also shown signs of weakness, as employment has failed to grow this year. Servus Credit Union chief economist Charles St-Arnaud said the stagnant labour market in recent months may be to blame for weaker retail sales.

“This is another indicator that suggests that the Canadian economy is losing momentum going into the last few months of 2026. The weakness suggests the Bank of Canada should take a pause to better assess the situation before hike again, especially with some fuel prices easing in recent weeks,” St-Arnaud said in an email.

Despite the expected slowdown, the Bank of Canada raised interest rates in October to clamp down on inflationary pressures from higher energy prices. Traders in overnight swaps put the odds of a hike in December at about 60%, which would further weigh on spending.

Despite the expected slowdown, the Bank of Canada raised interest rates in October to clamp down on inflationary pressures from higher energy prices. Traders in overnight swaps put the odds of a hike in December at about 60%, which would further weigh on spending.
–With assistance from Mario Baker Ramirez.

news.title: Google's Gemini can now run Mac apps and finish desktop chores in the background while you keep working
news.title_en: Google's Gemini can now run Mac apps and finish desktop chores in the background while you keep working
news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.article_content:
Google now lets Gemini handle Mac tasks in the background. The new "Computer Use"feature in the Gemini Mac app completes multistep tasks across local files, desktop apps, and websites. Google says users simply describe a goal, and Gemini clicks, types, and navigates menus and forms. Everything runs in an isolated background window with a live chat preview, keeping the screen and cursor free for uninterrupted work.

Users choose which apps Gemini can access, watch every step live, pause anytime, and approve key actions beforehand. Google's examples include batch-editing photos and 3D scenes, filling out shipping forms from local PDFs, and building presentations.

Computer Use rolls out in English in the US today, and the Gemini Mac app is available to download. OpenAI has also focused on Computer Use recently, pulling well ahead with its Astra model.

news.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
news.title_en: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
news.author: Lauren Feiner
news.article_content:
President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them.

“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.”

Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.”

Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative.

news.title: YouTube Finalizing Multibillion-Dollar Settlement With Schools Over Social Media Addiction Claims
news.title_en: YouTube Finalizing Multibillion-Dollar Settlement With Schools Over Social Media Addiction Claims
news.author: Bloomberg
news.article_content:
YouTube has reached an agreement in principle to pay around $3B to thousands of US school districts that accuse it of harming students’ mental health, Bloomberg reported. The deal includes new safeguards for teens and needs most districts to sign on.

YouTube is finalising a settlement of around $3B with thousands of US school districts, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. The districts accuse it of building an addictive platform that harmed students’ mental health.

It would be the largest corporate settlement ever reached with US school districts. The agreement in principle also includes new safeguards for teens. Google declined to comment, as did the lawyers leading the districts’ cases.

The deal needs a majority of the districts to sign on and will likely take a few months to finalise. The districts want money back for the costs of social media addiction, such as extra counselling for students. Schools are a key market for Google, which also faces pushback from its own staff over AI in student Search.

More than 10,000 lawsuits have been filed against YouTube, Meta, Snap and TikTok over the past five years. They claim features such as endless scrolling and autoplay have caused addiction, anxiety and depression in young people. Earlier this year, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube liable in the first bellwether trial.

Meta agreed in August to settle with nearly every US state for about $18B, by its own count, and to cap teens’ scrolling at two hours a day. In May, YouTube paid just over $2M to a Kentucky school district that also sued Meta, Snap and TikTok. In June, it settled with a teenager to avoid a second California trial.

The next school case, brought by a district in Tucson, Arizona, is due to go to trial in February. Meta, TikTok and Snap remain defendants.

The proposed settlement is valued at approximately $3 billion, with final execution expected to take several months.

paragraphs: YouTube has reached an agreement in principle to pay around $3B to thousands of US school districts that accuse it of harming students’ mental health, Bloomberg reported. The deal includes new safeguards for teens and needs most districts to sign on.

YouTube is finalising a settlement of around $3B with thousands of US school districts, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. The districts accuse it of building an addictive platform that harmed students’ mental health.

It would be the largest corporate settlement ever reached with US school districts. The agreement in principle also includes new safeguards for teens. Google declined to comment, as did the lawyers leading the districts’ cases.

The deal needs a majority of the districts to sign on and will likely take a few months to finalise. The districts want money back for the costs of social media addiction, such as extra counselling for students. Schools are a key market for Google, which also faces pushback from its own staff over AI in student Search.

More than 10,000 lawsuits have been filed against YouTube, Meta, Snap and TikTok over the past five years. They claim features such as endless scrolling and autoplay have caused addiction, anxiety and depression in young people. Earlier this year, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube liable in the first bellwether trial.

Meta agreed in August to settle with nearly every US state for about $18B, by its own count, and to cap teens’ scrolling at two hours a day. In May, YouTube paid just over $2M to a Kentucky school district that also sued Meta, Snap and TikTok. In June, it settled with a teenager to avoid a second California trial.
The next school case, brought by a district in Tucson, Arizona, is due to go to trial in February. Meta, TikTok and Snap remain defendants.

news.title: Trump says he would block US companies from building data centers overseas or impose a "tremendous tax" on them if they do (Julianna Bragg/Axios)

news.author: Axios
news.article_content:
President Trump on Friday said he would block U.S. companies from building data centers overseas or impose a "tremendous tax" on them if they do.

Why it matters: Trump's push to keep AI infrastructure in the country comes just weeks after data center expansion became a midterm-election flashpoint, as voters raised concerns about the environmental and financial impacts they pose.

What they're saying: Trump acknowledged that the announcement may come as a surprise, saying he had not yet discussed it with his own officials.

Reality check: It's unclear how Trump would implement the proposed tax, since Congress has the Constitutional authority to impose federal taxes.

Thought bubble from Axios' Ina Fried: Even companies that build data centers in the U.S. often need to have them in other places in order to have reliability, low latency and comply with various laws that require data to be processed in a specific region or country.

Friction point: Trump's remarks followed a trilateral summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin, but seemed torn between praising Xi and warning about the threats China poses to the U.S.

Yes, but: Trump also said Xi respected and congratulated the U.S. on its achievements in what he calls "super intelligence."

news.summary_en: Former President Donald Trump proposed a policy aimed at anchoring AI infrastructure within the U.S., threatening to block American companies from constructing data centers abroad or imposing heavy taxes if they do so. This policy stance follows heightened voter concern over the environmental and financial impacts of domestic data center expansion, though the legal mechanism for implementing such taxes remains unclear given Congressional oversight.

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 该政策倾向忽视了全球分布式计算对低延迟、数据驻留合规及灾备冗余的刚性商业需求，强制回流可能导致美国科技企业在国际市场失去交付效率竞争优势。短期内此类言论更偏向政治叙事，若转化为行政指令，将引发全球云服务供应链的剧烈重组与合规成本激增。

news.author: Julian E. Barnes, Paul Mozur, and Ana Swanson
news.article_content:
Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal, has extensive ties through her family and associates to China’s defense industry, according to an independent research firm and corporate filings reviewed by The New York Times.

The findings show a web of relationships, most of them indirect, linking Ms. Huang’s family and companies that acquired Nvidia chips to Chinese state-owned defense contractors that supply the People’s Liberation Army.

The nature of those relationships, including the vital question of whether Nvidia chips ended up being used to support Chinese military projects, remains murky. But the revelations, along with an investigation by The Times published on Wednesday, underscore how the Chinese effort to acquire access to the computing power of Nvidia’s chips is intertwined with Beijing’s desire to harness artificial intelligence to bolster its military capabilities.

That outcome has long been feared by U.S. national security officials, given that the technology could help China develop more sophisticated weapons, carry out cyberattacks and integrate A.I. into the battlefield.

A confidential analysis by Strider Technologies, an independent intelligence firm that employs former intelligence officers and experts on China and specializes in corporate intelligence, shows that about $3.6 billion in Chinese government money flowed through companies associated with Ms. Huang’s family or associates. The government money funded technology projects, including data centers that received Nvidia chips.

The New York Times reviewed the Strider findings. Many of the corporate ties revealed by Strider were independently confirmed by The Times.

The Times reported last month that U.S. officials believe Ms. Huang, a Chinese citizen also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese intelligence asset who was providing information to the Ministry of State Security. The Strider Technologies analysis and the review of corporate filings by The Times show that she; her sister, Huang Yu; and an investor named Kang Wei, who was Alice Huang’s business partner and often introduced as her husband, are tied to a web of companies that connect official Nvidia partners, which can buy advanced Nvidia A.I. chips, to state- and military-linked projects.

Nvidia’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, stepped down as the company’s chief executive after acknowledging an affair with Alice Huang, who is no relation.

paragraphs: Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal, has extensive ties through her family and associates to China’s defense industry, according to an independent research firm and corporate filings reviewed by The New York Times.

The findings show a web of relationships, most of them indirect, linking Ms. Huang’s family and companies that acquired Nvidia chips to Chinese state-owned defense contractors that supply the People’s Liberation Army.

The nature of those relationships, including the vital question of whether Nvidia chips ended up being used to support Chinese military projects, remains murky. But the revelations, along with an investigation by The Times published on Wednesday, underscore how the Chinese effort to acquire access to the computing power of Nvidia’s chips is intertwined with Beijing’s desire to harness artificial intelligence to bolster its military capabilities.

That outcome has long been feared by U.S. national security officials, given that the technology could help China develop more sophisticated weapons, carry out cyberattacks and integrate A.I. into the battlefield.

A confidential analysis by Strider Technologies, an independent intelligence firm that employs former intelligence officers and experts on China and specializes in corporate intelligence, shows that about $3.6 billion in Chinese government money flowed through companies associated with Ms. Huang’s family or associates. The government money funded technology projects, including data centers that received Nvidia chips.
The New York Times reviewed the Strider findings. Many of the corporate ties revealed by Strider were independently confirmed by The Times.

The Times reported last month that U.S. officials believe Ms. Huang, a Chinese citizen also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese intelligence asset who was providing information to the Ministry of State Security. The Strider Technologies analysis and the review of corporate filings by The Times show that she; her sister, Huang Yu; and an investor named Kang Wei, who was Alice Huang’s business partner and often introduced as her husband, are tied to a web of companies that connect official Nvidia partners, which can buy advanced Nvidia A.I. chips, to state- and military-linked projects.
Nvidia’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, stepped down as the company’s chief executive after acknowledging an affair with Alice Huang, who is no relation.

Companies in the Huang family’s network co-own a cybersecurity venture with an arm of China’s main military-electronics conglomerate, lease Nvidia-powered servers financed by an affiliate of its largest military aircraft maker and in one case share a parent company with a maker of radar and missile components.

Two companies that have partnerships with Nvidia, Megaspeed and Century Litong, are connected to Ms. Huang. Ms. Huang ran Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center firm that is under investigation by the Justice Department for smuggling advanced chips into China. Megaspeed has said Ms. Huang, whose involvement with Mr. Huang corresponded with a period when it was acquiring large numbers of Nvidia chips, no longer works for the company.

Ms. Huang’s family members had prominent roles and significant investments in the data center firm that founded Century Litong, which is based in Shanghai and rents out computing power to major Chinese companies and military contractors. The family members include Ms. Huang’s sister and Mr. Kang.

U.S. officials are also working to learn more about Ms. Huang and her efforts to help supply chips to data centers. The nature and extent of her ties to the P.L.A. and the companies it controls are a focus of that work, according to people briefed on the American efforts.

The ties are complex and often indirect. The research does not show whether the P.L.A. used computing power in the data centers that the family’s companies helped build. But it shows how deeply Ms. Huang and her family are intertwined with the Chinese state, and the inextricable connections between China’s tech industry and its military.

“Beijing has spent years building these networks that reach deep into Western economies,” said Greg Levesque, the chief executive of Strider. “Follow the money and, too often, you find the P.L.A. at the end of it.”

Mr. Levesque said China was exploiting more Western technology, capital and talent than ever before to build its defense industrial base. “This is happening on a scale we simply weren’t seeing a few years ago,” he said.
Nvidia declined to comment. Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment. Ms. Huang could not be reached for comment.

From late last year into early this year, Century Litong appears to have been one of only a few sources able to supply Nvidia chips to China at the vast scale needed for its A.I. build-out, according to Strider.

Those chips were key to building the data centers that drive China’s A.I. development. Investigators are trying to determine how many of the chips that were used in those data centers were banned under U.S. export controls and, in essence, smuggled into the country. Companies controlled by Ms. Huang and her relatives were instrumental in supplying the chips, Strider found.
“Essentially, those entities worked around the controls to continue to meet the chip demands of the customers they already had, including at new data centers,” Mr. Levesque said.

On Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee took the unusual step of releasing confidential information on Nvidia’s license applications to legally sell H200 chips to Chinese firms. The list showed that Nvidia had sought permission to sell more than 40,000 H200s to the Hong Kong subsidiary of Century Litong.
An Nvidia spokesman said that, despite receiving some licenses, it had already stopped shipping H200s to China, and Nvidia had not and would not ship to that firm.

Century Litong has said it has no business dealings with Ms. Huang. But the company was founded in 2023 by Century Longteng, a data center operator that was then 27 percent owned by an investment firm controlled by Ms. Huang’s sister. Mr. Kang, Ms. Huang’s presumed husband, had been Century Longteng’s executive director since February 2022, according to Strider.

In 2023, Jiangsu Lettall Electronic, a Shanghai-listed maker of metal parts for flat-screen TVs, bought 90 percent of Century Litong, and owned all of it by 2024. Lettall also owns 80 percent of Nanjing Jinning Microwave, a maker of components that Lettall has said are used in Chinese radar and missile systems. Strider said Jinning’s parts go into the P.L.A.’s DF-series missiles, including intercontinental ballistic missiles and anti-ship “carrier killers,” as well as the J-20 stealth fighter plane.
China’s defense industry wants advanced A.I. chips to design better missiles and build other military software, experts have said.

Lettall did not respond to an emailed request for comment. Asked about Ms. Huang’s network of companies and their efforts to acquire chips, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington said he was not familiar with the situation. “We have made clear more than once our principled position on U.S. chip exports to China,” said the spokesman, Liu Chang.

Century Litong delivered servers containing Nvidia’s H800 chips to a supercomputing center in Shanghai in October 2023, according to Strider. It is unclear where Century Litong obtained those chips, but they may have been obtained legally, since U.S. restrictions on the sale of the H800 to China did not go into effect until that same month.

Century Litong now runs servers at the Shanghai supercomputing center under a lease of about $54 million from a leasing arm of the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, China’s state aerospace and defense conglomerate.

Century Litong’s reach extends far beyond the Chinese A.I. giant Tencent. When Lettall bought into the company in 2023, it said all of Century Litong’s computing business would be housed in two places: the Tencent center in Shanghai and a data center in Shenzhen.

The Shenzhen center was built for the cloud unit of Huawei, the Chinese telecom giant that has long been under sanctions by the United States over national security concerns. Huawei awarded the project in 2022 to a company controlled by Century Longteng, according to corporate filings.

Century Litong’s customers have also included a unit of China Electronics Technology Group, or C.E.T.C., a state-owned military electronics maker. The United States has included C.E.T.C. on its list of companies that it publicly identifies as doing work with the Chinese military, banning the firm from doing work with Pentagon suppliers.
Another Century Litong partner is Hangjin Technology, a listed company whose subsidiaries make chips for China’s military.

Until last December, Hangjin controlled Chaoqing, an Nvidia partner whose website once listed High-Flyer, the hedge fund behind the Chinese A.I. start-up DeepSeek, as a partner. Others on the list included the military-linked Zhejiang Lab and its co-founder, Alibaba.

DeepSeek has attracted attention for its cutting-edge A.I. models. But lawmakers in the United States have also accused it of presenting national security risks, and the federal government has banned employees from using it. The Information earlier reported ties between Ms. Huang’s network and DeepSeek.
Hangjin did not respond to an emailed request for comment. It has said it does no business with DeepSeek.

news.summary_zh: 黄乐及其关联公司被指通过复杂网络获取英伟达芯片，资金流向与中国军工及国家安全部门存在高度关联

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 情报分析公司Strider Technologies发现，黄乐（Alice Huang）及其家族成员通过关联企业构建复杂网络，涉及约36亿美元中国政府资金，用于建设接收英伟达高性能AI芯片的数据中心。调查显示该网络不仅涉及中国国家安全部背景，更与中国军队防务承包商存在供应链交叉，引发英伟达芯片流向军事科研项目的重大合规风险。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Intelligence firm Strider Technologies identified that Alice Huang and her associates built a complex network utilizing $3.6 billion in Chinese government funding for data centers equipped with Nvidia AI chips. The investigation reveals that these entities maintain deep ties to Chinese military contractors and the Ministry of State Security, posing significant compliance risks regarding the diversion of restricted hardware into military research.

ai_analysis.insight_en: This case highlights significant loopholes in verifying end-users for High-Performance Computing (HPC) clusters, proving that entity-based trade controls are insufficient against complex, opaque corporate structures. As civil-military fusion deepens, the compliance burden for Nvidia and peers will shift from point-of-sale verification to full lifecycle traceability and forensic auditing of computational resource allocation.

news.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
news.title_en: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
news.author: Grace Huckins
news.article_content:
A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , due to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than the tasks in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt the task many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential to AI systems automating research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month weeks ago, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI capabilities progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

paragraphs: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , due to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than the tasks in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt the task many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential to AI systems automating research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month weeks ago, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI capabilities progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to incorporate some of these fuzzier, judgment-laden tasks that could be most relevant to AI research and development into their new suite. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about the extent to which the task is relevant for AI R&D automation. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even more so to determine what these scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into their work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”

Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees ask them to do as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original task suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising research questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck to AI R&D automation, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”

Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”

In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the tasks most relevant to AI R&D automation. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people to complete tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time consuming.

It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move towards open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

news.author: Lindsay Wise and Amrith Ramkumar
news.article_content:
WASHINGTON—Howard Lutnick repeatedly ignored warnings that U.S. artificial-intelligence chips were being smuggled to China before the recent Nvidia scandal became public, a top Republican senator said, the latest sign that lawmakers are blaming the Commerce Department for the potential security crisis.

In an interview, Sen. Tom Cotton (R., Ark.), a longtime China hawk who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, stopped short of saying Lutnick should resign or be fired as Commerce secretary, but he declined to support him.

news.author: Reuters
news.article_content:
Reporting the Changing World

US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed that humans should always be involved in military decisions made by artificial intelligence, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday.

“I think it was very important that the President Trump, and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” Bessent told CNBC, using the term “SI,” or superintelligence, for the technology.

Bessent said there was also “very robust discussion on what can be done in terms of containing the growth of nuclear weapons.”

He said the leaders held “a robust discussion on trade policy, AI,” and discussed the Russia-Ukraine war with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump, Xi and Putin met Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. In a joint declaration after the meeting, the three leaders reaffirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”

ai_analysis.insight_en: Establishing a 'human-in-the-loop' mandate for AI military decisions shifts the arms race from pure performance metrics to structural governance control. news.title: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
news.title_en: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
news.author: Robert Hart and Emma Roth
news.article_content:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.

Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday.

The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.

A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:

The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”

Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”

In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.

OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.

paragraphs: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.

Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday.

The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:

The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”

Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”

In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.

OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.

OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.

Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

celebrity.title: Oracle says it has secured funding for its infrastructure contract with OpenAI and "any further private discussions with vendors are just additional options" (@oracle)
celebrity.title_zh: 甲骨文完成OpenAI算力基建融资
celebrity.author: @oracle
celebrity.author_role: AI 先锋观察者
celebrity.summary_en: Oracle officially confirmed that it has secured the necessary funding to fulfill its artificial intelligence infrastructure contract with OpenAI. The company stated that any ongoing private discussions with potential vendors serve only as options for technical optimization rather than a requirement for project financing.
celebrity.summary_zh: 甲骨文公开确认已针对OpenAI基础设施合同锁定融资渠道，强调后续供应商谈判仅作为方案备选。
celebrity.full_text_zh: Oracle 表示，它已经为与 OpenAI 的基础设施合同获得了资金，“与供应商的任何进一步的私下讨论都只是额外的选择”
celebrity.full_text_en: Oracle says it has secured funding for its infrastructure contract with OpenAI and "any further private discussions with vendors are just additional options" (@oracle)

ai_analysis.insight_en: This move marks the transition of cloud infrastructure competition from pure resource leasing to high-density capital battles, where Oracle leverages upfront funding to secure high-value clients like OpenAI and erode Microsoft’s exclusive cloud dominance. Amidst GPU supply constraints, Oracle is attempting to bypass simple reseller models by building independent AI cloud foundations, directly capturing control over core model training workloads.

celebrity.full_text_en:
F*ck. Rockstar just permanently banned my Social Club account

i waited 13 years for this game. i was 17 when GTA 5 came out, i'm 30 now. they took it from me in less than 24 hours, and honestly i had it coming

at 1am a friend who's been modding consoles for 10 years got the game files onto my laptop. 200 GB of folders with names like "x64_core_7". no human reads that in a week

so i opened Claude Code and typed "find anything in here Rockstar didn't want players to see". 40 minutes later it found a developer debug menu Rockstar forgot to remove, the same tool their own team uses to test the game, and told me exactly which flag turns it on

with it you can fly anywhere on the map, spawn any car, skip any mission. so i skipped all of them and went straight to the finale. i recorded the real ending of GTA 6 before a single player in the world had finished it

at 8am i posted it on X. by noon it had 2 million views. half the replies begged me to delete it, the other half begged for more. one guy offered me $5,000 for the debug menu

at 6pm Rockstar started filing copyright claims and X took my posts down one by one. i got scared and deleted the rest myself

didn't help. at 11:47 PM this email hit my inbox. permanent ban with no appeal. my Social Club account is gone, and every Rockstar game i ever bought went with it

The ending was worth it. but the ending isn't the strangest thing in that menu. check the replies
celebrity.full_text_zh:
操。 Rockstar 刚刚永久禁止了我的 Social Club 帐户

我为了这款游戏等了13年。 GTA 5 发行时我 17 岁，现在我 30 岁了。他们在不到 24 小时内就从我这里拿走了它，说实话，我已经收到了

凌晨 1 点，一位从事游戏机改装 10 年的朋友将游戏文件放到了我的笔记本电脑上。 200 GB 的文件夹，名称如“x64_core_7”。一周内没有人读到它

所以我打开 Claude Code 并输入“在这里找到 Rockstar 不想让玩家看到的任何内容”。 40 分钟后，它发现了一个开发者调试菜单，Rockstar 忘记删除了，他们自己的团队使用同样的工具来测试游戏，并准确地告诉我哪个标志打开了它

celebrity.full_text_en:
This is f*cking insane.

you're spending days modeling, cleaning and exporting 3d characters by hand while claude code can drive most of the open source tools that do it for you.

One tool models. One fixes the topology. One unwraps the UVs. One paints the textures. One shrinks it for the game.

Here are 14 GitHub projects to build your own AI 3D modeling pipeline:

CLAUDE x BLENDER

01 / Blender MCP → Lets Claude drive Blender and build or edit models from a prompt.
https://t.co/rbJgtnd6Rf

02 / Blender Skills → 28 skills that teach Claude modeling, UVs, rigging and LODs.
https://t.co/0oN0s6ZAPE

MODELING

03 / build123d → Model props in Python code with clean booleans and fillets.
https://t.co/eBSr6L5Flb

04 / Building Tools → Blender add-on that generates buildings for your levels.
https://t.co/XlCuaX4yCU

05 / Tripo for Blender → Official add-on that generates a 3D model inside Blender.
https://t.co/nHk26A9ZxH

06 / Tripo Python SDK → Lets Claude call Tripo from a script.
https://t.co/DSOOEjflLv

RETOPO & CLEANUP

07 / AutoRemesher → Turns a heavy mesh into clean quads automatically.
https://t.co/eUPpuWlIio

08 / RetopoFlow → Hand retopology tools inside Blender.
https://t.co/aG04qULkam

09 / PyMeshLab → Mesh cleanup and repair that Claude can script.
https://t.co/wIN6GUcSEQ

UVs & TEXTURES

10 / xatlas → Automatic UV unwrap and packing.
https://t.co/UaaJarVBbd

11 / Material Maker → Free procedural PBR materials.
https://t.co/X4PdCE89S8

12 / ArmorPaint → Open source PBR texture painting.
https://t.co/Ypyv8W095T

LODs & EXPORT

13 / meshoptimizer → Decimates and compresses meshes for game LODs.
https://t.co/hIecvYR50V

14 / glTF-Transform → Scriptable optimizer for the final export.
https://t.co/MCL6kE3FED

celebrity.full_text_en:
update: the GTA VI PC port is already running Rockstar's PS5 code

last time i pulled 400 commits from AnyPS5. 
this time i read every commit since August

39 of them are about GTA V. the PS5 build of it, running through AnyPS5 on Nvidia cards

Sept 29 → GTA V runs at 0.1 fps
Oct 15 → the bank prologue, about 20 fps on a 5080
Oct 16 → Story mode, 16.47 fps on a 4090

28 of those 39 commits are co-authored by Claude

some aren't even humans with AI help. 

the authors are literally named "m2 (AI Agent)", "Cursor Agent", "Hermes Agent"

the repo went from 71 commits in August to 17,627 in October

> right side: GTA V commits, with the fps lines in green
> left side: every commit flying past, orange means Claude co -wrote it

GTA V is the rehearsal. same studio, same console

the day someone dumps GTA VI
this machine is already warmed up ↓

tools.article_content:
The Justice and Commerce Departments said that they are investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center company intertwined with the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, after reporting suggested an investigation had been halted last year.

“While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting,” the departments said in a statement issued Monday evening. The departments acknowledged there’s been “significant public attention” on Megaspeed.

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week after reports he had an affair with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, who Megaspeed says left the company in August 2025. The scandal has raised questions about national security, and sparked scrutiny of Nvidia’s handling of exports of its chips to China and Megaspeed’s possible role in moving along Nvidia’s chips.

Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed “came to a sudden halt” late last year after its investigators received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel, claiming Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler gave Nvidia permission to reach out. The case was then “quickly” handed over to the DOJ, according to the Times.

> After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list. Based on the Department of Commerce’s investigation, agents from the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang. Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

The statement doesn’t go into detail about the current status of the case, but it says the DOJ and Commerce Department “will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 美国司法部与商务部发布声明，确认正就出口管制违规嫌疑对新加坡数据中心企业Megaspeed进行调查。该调查动因涉及前Nvidia CEO黄仁勋辞职引发的公职安全关注，以及该公司在Nvidia芯片流向受限地区过程中的中介角色，目前美方正结合新加坡执法力量进行穿透式审查。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: The U.S. DOJ and Commerce Department have confirmed an investigation into Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed regarding potential export control violations. Triggered by national security scrutiny following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the investigation probes Megaspeed's intermediary role in the potential diversion of Nvidia chips, with joint enforcement efforts involving Singaporean authorities.

elements_zh.where: 美国与新加坡境内
elements_zh.what: 对Megaspeed进行出口管制合规性与最终用途检查
elements_zh.why: 应对Nvidia芯片可能受限流转引发的国家安全担忧

elements_en.who: U.S. DOJ, BIS of the Commerce Department, Megaspeed (former executive Alice Huang)
elements_en.what: Investigation into export control compliance and end-use of chips
elements_en.why: National security concerns regarding potential diversion of restricted Nvidia hardware

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 此次调查将供应链合规性锚点从芯片分销商前移至数据中心运营商，标志着美方对高性能算力基础设施的“长臂管辖”已进入深水区。对Megaspeed的穿透式审计，将实质性重构东南亚算力基建商的合规风控成本，并可能迫使Nvidia及类似半导体巨头全面重组其海外渠道准入标准。
ai_analysis.insight_en: This investigation shifts compliance scrutiny from chip distributors to data center operators, signaling an expansion of U.S. extraterritorial oversight over high-performance computing infrastructure. The penetration audit of Megaspeed will likely reshape compliance costs for Southeast Asian data infrastructure and force semiconductor giants to restructure their international channel access protocols.
